guides.title: Why construct correct programs?
paragraphs: This course (CS601, Advanced Topics in Software Engineering) attacks the verification problem by constructing a correct program a step at a time, using a theory of programming.

Industry keeps shipping failures: budget overruns, late delivery, and outages (Meta, NYSE, CrowdStrike/Microsoft, exchanges, airports). The point of the opening slides is not the news — it is that “test at the end” is not enough for critical systems.
bullets: Prove each development step as you write it.
When you modify a program, prove the modification is still correct.
Targets: protocols, kernels, compilers, medical/nuclear/railway/aerospace — anywhere human life or large money is at risk.
guides.trap: Memorizing disaster stories is not the exam skill. The exam skill is precise specifications and proofs.

check.prompt: In this course, how do we tackle verification?
choices: By constructing a program step by step and proving each step
check.explainCorrect: Stepwise construction with proof is the course objective.
check.explainWrong: We prove as we develop — not only test at the end.

guides.title: What the theory claims
paragraphs: A mathematical theory of programming gives calculation precision and a scientific understanding of programs (like theorems, not folklore).

In Hehner’s theory used here: a specification is a binary expression; refinement is implication. The same framework later covers terminating and nonterminating, sequential and concurrent, stand-alone and interactive computation.

check.prompt: In this theory, refinement is…
check.explainWrong: Keep the slogan: specs are binary; refine by ⇒.

guides.title: Binary theory — two kinds
paragraphs: Binary theory is also called Boolean algebra / propositional calculus. Binary expressions classify into theorems and antitheorems (two kinds).
The two simplest values: ⊤ (theorem / top / true) and ⊥ (antitheorem / bottom / false). Analogies in the slides: power/ground, innocent/guilty.
guides.example: You may leave some expressions unclassified (incomplete theory), but you must never classify the same expression as both theorem and antitheorem (inconsistent).
guides.trap: Unclassified ≠ antitheorem. “We do not know / do not care” is allowed; contradiction is not.

check.prompt: Which property is essential?
choices: Every expression must be classified immediately
No expression is both theorem and antitheorem (consistency)
check.explainCorrect: Consistency is required; completeness is a choice.

guides.title: Operators you must read fluently
paragraphs: One operand: ¬ (not). Two operands: ∧ (and / conjunction), ∨ (or / disjunction), ⇒ (implies; antecedent ⇒ consequent), ⇐ (implied by), = and ≠.
Three operands: if x then a else b fi (conditional composition).
Ordering reading (slides): ⇒ means “stronger than or equal / lower-or-equal in the Boolean order”; ⇐ is the reverse ordering.
formulas: if x then a else b fi
bullets: ∧ and ∨ are associative.
Material implication law you will use constantly: x ⇒ y  ≡  ¬x ∨ y.
Use spacing and parentheses carefully: prefer x∧y ∨ z over ambiguous spacing.

check.prompt: Expand implication with the material-implication law:

guides.title: Truth table — evaluate when parts are known
guides.slidesRef: Lecture One · Evaluation of binary notations
paragraphs: When every subexpression is classified, classify the whole expression from the operator tables (Evaluation idea — fully stated as a proof rule in Lecture Two).

check.prompt: Classify each expression:
check.explainCorrect: Or needs one ⊤; and needs both; false⇒anything holds; true⇒false fails.

guides.title: Instantiation and classification in an application
paragraphs: Substitution (instantiation): replace variables by expressions. From x∧y you may form (⊥⇒¬(⊥∨⊤)) ∧ (⊥∨⊤).
An application (grass is green, sky is green, life elsewhere, …) must classify new expressions as theorem, antitheorem, or leave them unclassified — but stay consistent.
Number example from slides: 1+1=2 is a theorem; 1+1>2 antitheorem; 1/0=5 may stay unclassified.

guides.title: Five proof rules — overview
paragraphs: Proving means classifying a binary expression as theorem or antitheorem. Classical logic in this course uses five rules.
Constructive logic drops Completion; evaluation-style logics also drop Consistency. You use the classical five.
bullets: 1 Axiom: axioms are theorems; antiaxioms are antitheorems.
2 Evaluation: if all subexpressions are classified, use the truth tables.
3 Completion: if every way of classifying unknowns gives the same class, the whole expression has that class.
4 Consistency: if the whole is classified and only one classification of the parts is consistent, take that one.
5 Instance: a classified expression’s instances inherit that classification.

check.prompt: You know every part’s class and compute the whole from tables. Which rule?
check.explainCorrect: Evaluation = truth tables on known parts.

guides.title: Axiom and Evaluation
paragraphs: Binary theory axiom ⊤ and antiaxiom ⊥. Application axioms (slides): “grass is green” theorem; “sky is green” antitheorem; implication about intelligent messages may be an axiom.
Evaluation: if operands are known, tables decide the operator result.
guides.example: If a=⊤ and b=⊥ then a∧b is ⊥ by Evaluation.

check.prompt: The only antiaxiom of pure binary theory is…

guides.title: Completion rule (case analysis)
paragraphs: If subexpressions are unknown, but every possible classification makes the whole the same class, Completion classifies the whole.
Slide example: “life elsewhere ∨ ⊤” is a theorem either way (⊤∨⊤ or ⊥∨⊤).
Also: a ∨ ¬a is always ⊤; a ∧ ¬a is always ⊥ — by trying both classes for a.
guides.example: Theorem by Completion: a ∨ ¬a. Antitheorem by Completion: a ∧ ¬a.

check.prompt: Why is (unknown) ∨ ⊤ a theorem?
choices: By Completion: both cases end as ⊤
check.explainCorrect: Both classifications of the unknown give ⊤.

guides.title: Consistency rule (work backwards)
paragraphs: Now the whole expression is already classified; you ask what the parts must be. Only one consistent way is allowed.
Example: x and (x⇒y) are theorems → y cannot be ⊥ (that would make x⇒y antitheorem) → y is a theorem.
Example: ¬x is a theorem → x cannot be ⊤ → x is antitheorem. Slide moral: you can avoid separate “antiaxiom talk” by saying the negation is a theorem.

check.prompt: If ¬x is a theorem, Consistency forces x to be…
check.explainCorrect: If x were ⊤, ¬x would be ⊥ — contradiction.

guides.title: Instance rule + proof format
paragraphs: Instance: from classified x=x, every substitution instance is classified the same way.
Proof format: vertical calculation with hints on the right. Break long lines at the main connective. Prefer readable spacing around low-precedence operators.
guides.example: Prove a∧b ⇒ c ≡ a ⇒ (b ⇒ c) by material implication, duality, then reflexivity to ⊤.

check.prompt: Bad formatting habit called out in slides?
choices: Writing x∧y ∨ z with clear spaces / breaks
Writing x ∧ y∨z in a misleading way

guides.title: Inverse, converse, contrapositive
paragraphs: For A ⇒ B: converse is B ⇒ A; inverse is ¬A ⇒ ¬B. Neither equals the original in general.
Contrapositive ¬B ⇒ ¬A IS equivalent to A ⇒ B. Do not confuse contrapositive with converse.

check.prompt: Which is equivalent to A ⇒ B?

guides.title: Monotonicity, antimonotonicity, context
paragraphs: In the Boolean order, weaker/stronger matter. ¬ is antimonotonic in its argument. ∧ and ∨ are monotonic in both sides. In x⇒y, antimonotonic in x, monotonic in y.
Context rules: inside a ∧ B, when rewriting B you may assume a. Inside a ∨ B, assume ¬a when rewriting B. Inside a ⇒ B, assume a when rewriting B. Inside A ⇒ b, assume ¬b when rewriting A.
guides.example: ¬(a ∧ ¬(a∨b)): by generality a ⇒ a∨b, strengthen the inner part using monotonicity/context toward ⊤.
guides.trap: Rewriting a subexpression against monotonicity direction silently breaks the proof.

check.prompt: In a ⇒ B, when rewriting B you may assume…
check.explainCorrect: Antecedent is assumed in the consequent’s context.

guides.title: Formalism pitfalls (English → logic)
paragraphs: Programmers must translate vague English into formal binary expressions. Words “and/also/but/yet/however/moreover” often become ∧.
“Or” may be ∨ or exclusive ≠ depending on meaning. “If” may be ⇒ or = (biconditional intent).
guides.example: “If it rains, we stay home” ≈ rain ⇒ home (may stay home anyway). “If it snows, we can ski” may mean snow = ski.

check.prompt: “They’re red, ripe, juicy, but not sweet” formalizes mainly with…
check.explainWrong: Use ∧ for the list of properties.

guides.title: Number theory + domain addendum
paragraphs: Number expressions: digits, ∞, unary minus, + − × /, power, max ↑, min ↓, and if-then-else with a binary condition. Relations < ≤ > ≥ = ≠ produce binary expressions.
Number theory is incomplete: e.g. 1/0=5 and some root/complex cases may be unprovable either way.
Domain ladder (addendum): nat ⊂ int ⊂ rat ⊂ real, plus irrationals inside reals; imaginaries bi; complexes a+bi. Even roots of negatives leave reals.
bullets: rat = quotients a/b with b≠0
real = rational ∪ irrational
Character theory: “A”, succ/pred, order operators — small theory.

check.prompt: Which is true?
choices: Every number equation is classified in this course’s number theory
Number theory can leave some expressions unclassified (incomplete)
check.explainCorrect: Incompleteness is stated explicitly in the slides.

guides.title: Bunch theory — deep dive
paragraphs: Elementary bunches are elements (numbers, characters, binary values, later also sets/strings/lists as elements). Union A,B ; intersection A‘B ; size ¢A ; inclusion A:B.
Key slogan from slides: a bunch consists of its elements (it does not “contain” them the way a packaged set does).
bullets: x:y ≡ x=y (elementary)
x: A,B ≡ x:A ∨ x:B (compound)
Idempotence, symmetry, associativity for , and ‘
Colon : is an order (reflexive, antisymmetric, transitive) — like ≤ on numbers and ⇒ on binary
Useful bunches: null, bin, nat, int, rat, real, xnat/xint/…, char
x,..y for integers: i: x,..y ≡ x≤i<y ; ¢(x,..y)=y−x
guides.trap: ¢(A,B)+¢(A‘B)=¢A+¢B — size is not “idempotent counting of duplicates” in the naive bag sense; duplicates were already collapsed by bunch union.

check.prompt: 0,..3 equals…
check.explainWrong: Goes up to but not including 3.

guides.title: Set theory — packaging
paragraphs: S={A} packages bunch A. ~S is the contents (a bunch). Structure ≠ contents: {1,2,3,7} ≠ 1,2,3,7, yet ~{1,2,3,7}=1,2,3,7.
Cardinality ${A}=¢A. Power set example: ℘(0,1) = {null},{0},{1},{0,1}.
guides.example: {1,4,8}, 9 is a bunch of two elements (a set and a number). {{1,4,8},9} packages those two.

check.prompt: Which is correct?
choices: {1,2} and 1,2 are the same kind of value
{1,2} packages the bunch 1,2 into one set value

guides.title: String theory — indexed sequences
paragraphs: Strings are indexed sequences. nil empty; 4;5;8;9 a four-item string; ↔S length; Sn item at index n; S;T join; n*S copies; *S Kleene-style bunch of all copy-counts; S⊲n⊳i “same as S but index n is i”.
Order is lexicographic (like dictionary / digit strings).
guides.trap: Parentheses matter when mixing bunch comma with string join: (A,B);(D,E) distributes; A,B;D,E does not mean the same parse.

guides.title: List theory — packaged strings
paragraphs: A list is a string in a package — same idea as set vs bunch. [0;1;2] is a list. [ ] distributes over bunches: [A,B]=[A],[B].
Contents ~L is a string. Join lists with ;; . Modification n→i | L stores i at index n. Length #L ; domain ☐L = 0,..#L ; indexing L n.
guides.example: Swap idea: for L=[10;..15], 2→L3 | 3→L2 | L uses the original L in both readings — yields [10;11;13;12;14].

check.prompt: What is ~[3;5;7]?
check.explainCorrect: Contents of a list is a string.

guides.title: Multidimensional lists + function preview
paragraphs: A 2D list is a list of lists (array). Example A=[[6;3;7;0];[4;9;2;5];[1;5;8;3]] then A1=[4;9;2;5], A1 3=5.
Functions: succ = 〈v: D → v+1〉 with angled brackets for scope/domain. Application succ 7. Parentheses are reserved for other purposes in the notation — prefer juxtaposition.

cards.title: ok — the empty program
cards.plain: ok means “do nothing”: every variable’s final value equals its initial value. It is a precise specification, not a vague “true.”
cards.readAloud: ok leaves the whole state unchanged.
cards.confused: Trap: ok is not the same as ⊤. ⊤ allows any final state. ok allows only “no change.”

check.prompt: What is the difference between ok and ⊤ as specifications?
choices: ok requires unchanged state; ⊤ allows any final state
check.explainCorrect: ⊤ is the weakest possible binary claim; ok is specifically “no change.”
check.explainWrong: Never treat ok as interchangeable with ⊤.

cards.title: Assignment
cards.plain: x:= e is a program (and a specification) that sets final x to the value of e, computed in the initial state, and typically leaves other variables alone.
cards.example: x:= x + 1 has specification involving x′ = x + 1 (and other vars unchanged, depending on frame).

check.prompt: What does x:= 3 intend for x?

cards.title: Sequential composition
cards.plain: P.Q means do P, then Q. The final state after P becomes the initial state for Q. The period is sequential composition.
cards.example: x:= 1. x:= x + 1 ends with x′ = 2.

check.prompt: In P.Q, the initial state of Q is…
choices: The final state produced by P
check.explainCorrect: Outputs of P feed into Q.
check.explainWrong: Sequential means P finishes, then Q starts from there.

cards.title: Programs are specifications
cards.plain: In this theory, a program is a special kind of specification — one we know how to implement/execute. So programs sit inside the same logic.

check.prompt: A program in Hehner’s theory is…
check.explainCorrect: Programs are specifications with implementable shape.
check.explainWrong: Programs are a subclass of specifications.

cards.title: Refinement
cards.plain: Specification S is refined by P when every behavior of P is allowed by S. In the book this is the implication P ⇒ S (P is stronger / more specific).
cards.readAloud: P implies S — P is a refinement of S.
cards.confused: English “refine” means “make more precise.” A refining program may be harder to satisfy but still must obey the customer’s spec S.

check.prompt: If P refines S, which implication do we need?
check.explainCorrect: P ⇒ S: behaviors of P are included in those allowed by S.

proofs.title: ok refines? wait — ok implies weaker specs
proofs.claimReading: Doing nothing implies x is unchanged (among possibly more conjuncts).

wrongReasons.⇒: This step is an equality law for trailing ok.

drills.prompt: Does ⊤ refine ok? (Is ⊤ ⇒ ok a theorem?)
choices: No — ⊤ allows changes; ok forbids them
drills.explainCorrect: ⊤ is weaker; it does not imply ok.

drills.prompt: Show why x:= x is like ok for variable x (idea). Use hints.
hints: Assignment x:= x wants x′ = x (and others unchanged with proper frame).
That is exactly the conjuncts that make ok on those variables.
drills.solution: x:= x sets x′ = x (and leaves others unchanged under the usual frame). That is the same constraint ok places on x. So for that variable, x:= x matches ok.

cards.title: Specification laws
cards.plain: Specifications obey algebraic laws — you can rewrite them like logic expressions. That is how you simplify a customer requirement before coding.

check.prompt: Why learn specification laws?
choices: To rewrite and simplify specs safely
check.explainWrong: Use laws to transform specs without changing meaning.

cards.title: Refinement laws
cards.plain: Refinement has its own laws: if you refine a part correctly, you refine the whole in structured ways (sequential composition, if, etc.).
cards.notation: If P ⇒ S and Q ⇒ R then P.Q ⇒ S.R (under the theory’s conditions)

check.prompt: Refinement laws help you…

check.explainCorrect: Stepwise refinement is the development method.
check.explainWrong: You refine piece by piece toward a program.

cards.plain: A classic development: specify the sum of a list, then refine to a loop or recursion that accumulates the total.
cards.example: Spec idea: s′ = sum of list L (and other frame conditions).

proofs.claimReading: Repeating a specification conjunct does nothing.

drills.prompt: Outline why S ∧ S = S matters when cleaning a spec. Hints available.

Idempotence lets you delete repeated conjuncts.
drills.solution: If a behavior satisfies S, it satisfies S∧S and conversely. So repeated conjuncts can be dropped by idempotence without changing the meaning of the specification.

cards.title: Hoare triple idea

cards.title: Time in specifications
cards.plain: You can add a time variable (often t) to specifications so that a program must finish by a deadline or take a measured number of steps.

check.prompt: Why put time in a specification?
choices: To talk about duration and deadlines precisely
check.explainCorrect: Time becomes part of the before/after claim.

cards.title: Recursive time
cards.plain: For recursive programs, time often adds the cost of the recursive calls plus local work. The specification mentions how t grows.

check.prompt: Recursive time analysis connects…
choices: Call structure to added time in the spec
check.explainCorrect: Recursion depth/work shows up in t′.

cards.title: Termination
cards.plain: Termination means the computation reaches a final state. In this theory you prove it with the specification (often via a variant that decreases).
cards.confused: “It looks like it loops” is not a proof. You need a formal reason that progress is finite.

check.prompt: Which is NOT a termination argument?

A specification that forces t′ to be finite relative to t
Refinement to a loop with a proven variant
check.explainWrong: Need a formal variant / time argument.

drills.solution: Include a time variable in the state and write binary constraints relating final time t′ to initial time t (and the other variables), so duration becomes part of the specification.

cards.title: Scope and declaration
cards.plain: A variable declaration introduces a name with a local scope. Outside that region, the name is not available (or means something else).
cards.readAloud: Declare x of type T, then do P.

cards.title: Variable suspension
cards.plain: Suspension temporarily hides an outer variable so an inner region can reuse a name carefully. Beginner takeaway: nested scopes can shadow.

check.prompt: Inner declaration of x while outer x exists…
choices: Can hide/shadow the outer x in the inner region
Merges both into a bunch automatically

cards.title: Array
cards.plain: An array is a programmable list-like structure: indexed collection you can read and assign to at indices.
cards.notation: A i   or   A(i)   depending on notation

check.prompt: Assigning to index i of array A means…
choices: Change the i-th slot’s final value to e

cards.title: Record
cards.plain: A record groups named fields (like a struct). You select fields by name rather than by numeric index.

check.prompt: Records differ from arrays mainly by…
choices: Using named fields instead of only numeric indices

cards.title: While-loop
cards.plain: while b do P od repeats P as long as condition b holds. Its meaning is given by a specification/refinement law in the book — not by hand-waving.

check.prompt: A while-loop repeats while…

cards.title: Exit-loop & for-loop
cards.plain: Exit-loops allow leaving from the middle. For-loops iterate a known pattern (often over a range). Both have precise specification meanings.

check.prompt: Exit from the middle of a loop is associated with…
check.explainCorrect: Exit-loop is the construct for mid-exit.
check.explainWrong: Use exit-loop when control leaves mid-body.

cards.title: Functions and procedures
cards.plain: A function returns a value; a procedure is invoked for its effect on state. Both are subprograms with specifications.

check.prompt: Which pairing is right?
choices: Function ↔ value result; procedure ↔ state effect (typical)
check.explainCorrect: Classic distinction used in the chapter.
check.explainWrong: Functions yield values; procedures act on state.

cards.title: Toward the January review
cards.plain: By lecture Eleven you should connect: logic → data → specs → refinement → (later) time → programming constructs. Review-2026 on 3/1 is for tying it together.

Only memorize Unicode symbols with no checks

proofs.title: While when b is false
proofs.claim: If ¬b initially, while b do P od acts like ok
proofs.claimReading: No iterations → no state change from the loop body.

In one sentence: what must a while-loop refinement prove besides partial correctness? Hints OK.
hints: Termination / variant, especially when time matters.
drills.solution: Besides establishing the postcondition when it stops, you must ensure termination (e.g. a variant decreases), especially if the specification includes time or requires a final state.

cards.title: Substitution idea
cards.plain: Substitution means: in an expression, replace a variable by a value or another expression. Assignment and proof steps rely on this.
cards.example: In x′ = x + 1, if initial x is 4, the interesting final claim becomes x′ = 5.
cards.notation: E[x: e]  — “E with x replaced by e” (notation varies; learn the idea)

cards.title: Quantifiers in specs
cards.plain: ∀ means “for all.” ∃ means “there exists.” Specs sometimes say “for all indices…” or “there exists a final state…”
cards.readAloud: For every index i in range, list element L i is positive.

choices: Some natural n has n+0 = n
Every natural n has n+0 = n

cards.title: Functions as mappings
cards.plain: A function maps inputs to outputs. Lists are a special case: domain is an initial segment of naturals. You only need the beginner reading for now.

check.explainWrong: Lists behave as functions from positions to values.

proofs.claimReading: If P holds for all x, then it holds for a particular a.

glossary.name: top / true
glossary.reading: A theorem. The “always holds” binary value.

glossary.name: bottom / false
glossary.reading: An antitheorem. The “never holds” binary value.

glossary.name: and / conjunction
glossary.reading: Both sides must hold.

glossary.name: or / disjunction
glossary.reading: At least one side holds.

glossary.name: not / negation
glossary.reading: Flips theorem ↔ antitheorem.

glossary.name: implies
glossary.reading: If the left holds, so does the right. Read “left implies right.”

glossary.name: implied by
glossary.reading: The left follows from the right. Useful when driving a proof upward to ⊤.

glossary.name: equals
glossary.reading: Both sides have the same binary classification (or same value).

glossary.name: x prime
glossary.reading: The final value of state variable x. Plain x is the initial value.
glossary.tip: Before / after: x is start, x′ is end.

glossary.name: do nothing
glossary.reading: The empty program: every variable ends equal to how it started. σ′ = σ.
glossary.tip: Not the same as ⊤. ok is a specific specification about the state.

glossary.name: sequential composition
glossary.reading: P.Q means “do P, then do Q.” The final state of P is the initial state of Q.

glossary.name: assignment
glossary.reading: x:= e sets the final value of x to e (and usually leaves other variables alone).

glossary.name: bunch union (comma)
glossary.reading: In bunch theory, A,B is the bunch of elements from A or B (or both).

glossary.name: set packing
glossary.reading: A set packages a bunch. {1,2} is a single set value whose contents are the bunch 1,2.

glossary.name: function scope brackets
glossary.reading: 〈x: D → body〉 introduces a function with domain D. (Strings use semicolon sequences, not these brackets.)

glossary.name: list brackets
glossary.reading: A list packages a string: [0;1;2]. Contents ~L unpack back to a string.

glossary.name: bunch inclusion
glossary.reading: A:B means A is included in B (bunch order). Like ≤ on numbers and ⇒ on binary.

glossary.name: bunch union
glossary.reading: A,B is the union of bunches A and B (unpackaged, unindexed).

glossary.name: contents
glossary.reading: ~S / ~L unpacks a set or list to the underlying bunch or string.

glossary.name: bunch size
glossary.reading: ¢A is the cardinality of bunch A. Duplicates are already collapsed.

glossary.name: refinement (often written as implication)
glossary.reading: Specification S is refined by program P when P ⇒ S: every behavior of P is allowed by S.

midtermDrills.explainCorrect: False antecedent makes implication a theorem.
Braces pack a bunch into a set.

one.title: Animated: theorem vs antitheorem
one.summary: Step through what ⊤ and ⊥ mean before you watch the long Binary Theory video.

steps.title: Two buckets
steps.body: Every binary expression we care about is sorted into theorem (holds) or antitheorem (does not).

steps.title: And needs both
steps.body: ∧ is a theorem only when both sides are theorems.

steps.title: Or needs one
steps.body: ∨ is a theorem if at least one side is a theorem.

steps.title: Implication surprise
steps.body: If the left side is already ⊥, implication holds. The dangerous case is ⊤ ⇒ ⊥.

one.title: Animated: material implication
one.summary: The rewrite you will use constantly in proofs.

steps.title: Law
steps.body: Implication is defined/usable as “not antecedent, or consequent”.

steps.title: Why ⊥ ⇒ y is ⊤
steps.body: ¬⊥ ∨ y becomes ⊤ ∨ y which is ⊤.

steps.title: Use in a proof line
steps.body: When a calculation needs to expand ⇒, cite Material implication as the hint.
steps.visual:
a ⇒ a ∨ b
= ¬a ∨ (a ∨ b)     Material implication

two.title: Animated: which proof rule?
two.summary: A decision map for Axiom / Evaluation / Completion / Consistency / Instance.

steps.title: Axiom
steps.body: The expression is declared theorem or antitheorem (⊤ / ⊥, or an application axiom).

steps.title: Evaluation
steps.body: All parts are already classified → use the truth table.

steps.title: Completion
steps.body: Parts unknown, but every case gives the same class → that class.

steps.title: Consistency
steps.body: Whole is classified; only one story about the parts is consistent → take it.

steps.title: Instance
steps.body: A classified schema stays classified for every substitution instance.
steps.visual:
x = x is theorem
⇒ (⊤∨⊥)=(⊤∨⊥) is theorem

two.title: Animated: bunch vs set
two.summary: Packaging is the whole exam trap.

steps.title: Bunch = content
steps.body: 1,2,3 is the elements themselves (unpackaged, unindexed).

steps.title: Set = package
steps.body: {1,2,3} is one value that packs that bunch.

steps.title: Move between them
steps.body: ~ unpacks; { } packs.

three.title: Animated: four data structures
three.summary: Packaging × indexing table as a story.

steps.title: Bunch
steps.body: Unpackaged and unindexed — just elements with comma union.

steps.title: Set
steps.body: Packaged and unindexed — braces create one object.

steps.title: String
steps.body: Unpackaged and indexed — order and positions matter.

steps.title: List
steps.body: Packaged and indexed — a string inside list brackets.

three.title: Animated: x vs x′
three.summary: Initial vs final state — the #1 program-theory mistake.

steps.title: Before
steps.body: Unprimed variables are the starting state.

steps.title: After
steps.body: Primed variables are the ending state.

steps.title: A tiny spec
steps.body: “Increase x by 1 and leave y alone.”

four.title: Animated: ok vs ⊤ and refinement
four.summary: Do-nothing vs anything-goes, and which way ⇒ points.

steps.title: ok
steps.body: Every variable ends equal to how it started.

steps.title: ⊤ is weaker
steps.body: ⊤ allows any final state. So ⊤ does not imply ok.

steps.title: Refinement
steps.body: Program P refines spec S when P ⇒ S.
steps.visual:
P ⇒ S
“every behavior of P is allowed by S”
